How bot detection actually works

Most write-ups treat bot detection as a single check. In practice it is a stack of signals, and the interesting part is how they are combined.

The first signal is the TLS handshake. A client that claims to be Chrome but negotiates like a Go program is easy to separate from a real browser.

Header order matters too. Browsers emit headers in a stable order, and a client that sorts them alphabetically stands out even when every individual value is correct.

Here is the shape of a Cloudflare challenge configuration, which is what people usually mean when they say "the page is blocked":

window._cf_chl_opt = { cvId: '3', cType: 'managed' };

Vendors also run a captcha or a press & hold interaction when the score is ambiguous. Those are the visible part of the system, not the whole system.

A good scraper therefore does not try to win every fight. It sends a coherent identity, detects when it has been blocked, and reports that honestly instead of returning the challenge page as content.

That last point is underrated. A silent block is worse than a loud failure, because every downstream consumer treats the block page as data.
